title: Systematic Discrepancies Should Be Addressed Before Effective Parameter Learning: Insights From Soil Moisture Simulations Using Differentiable Process‐Based Models
content:
Abstract

Differentiable hydrologic models combining neural networks with process-based backbones—fully implemented or approximated by surrogate models—offer highly competitive accuracy and improved interpretability compared to either model type used alone. However, the impacts of surrogate model fidelity (accurate sensitivity of relationships compared to the original model) and systematic discrepancies between models and observations on parameter learning effectiveness remain underexplored. This study evaluates optimization performance of the differentiable HBV model (δHBV) and its surrogate variants in simulating soil moisture across the contiguous United States. Results show that high-fidelity surrogate models can support effective differentiable parameter learning once systematic discrepancies are addressed. In contrast, unresolved systematic discrepancies degrade optimization performance, with particularly severe deterioration when low-fidelity surrogates are used. These findings provide one possible explanation for the modest improvements reported in recent surrogate-based differentiable parameter learning (dPL) applications. Linear correction partially mitigates these systematic discrepancies, improves optimization performance, and reduces compensatory parameter adjustment, although it does not resolve the underlying model–observation mismatch. Structural refinement remains a physically grounded long-term direction, while pragmatic correction modules can provide useful partial mitigation when such refinement is not yet available. In addition, fully implementing differentiable process-based models or using a rigorously trained surrogate can improve gradient fidelity and reduce amplified deterioration associated with surrogate infidelity.
